lesson.title: The Circuit's Unbreakable Budget: Energy Conservation
lesson.summary: Every joule a source delivers to a circuit must show up somewhere else, as heat, stored energy, or useful work, because energy in a circuit obeys the same conservation law that governs all of physics.
lesson.body:
Physics has a rule that never bends: energy cannot be created or destroyed, only converted from one form to another. Circuits are no exception, and applying this rule to electrical systems gives you a powerful accounting tool. Whatever electrical energy a source, like a battery, supplies to a circuit over some period of time must be exactly matched by the energy that leaves the circuit through resistors as heat, through other components as stored energy, or through a load as useful work. Nothing is left over, and nothing appears from nowhere.

Because power is defined as the rate of energy transfer, energy over time, you can move between these two quantities using multiplication or division by time. If a device delivers power P for a duration t, the energy transferred is E equals P times t. This lets you convert between the instantaneous power calculations you have already learned and the total energy a circuit consumes or delivers over minutes, hours, or any interval you choose, which is exactly what your electric utility bill is measuring when it charges you for kilowatt hours.

Energy conservation in a circuit means that if you add up the power delivered by every source and multiply by the time interval, that total energy must equal the sum of the energy dissipated by every resistive element plus any energy stored in the circuit. In a simple resistive DC circuit with no capacitors or inductors, there is nowhere for energy to be stored, so every joule supplied becomes a joule of heat somewhere among the resistors. This gives you a built in accuracy check: if your calculated resistor dissipations do not add up to the source's output, you have made an arithmetic mistake somewhere in the circuit analysis.

Suppose a 12 volt battery delivers a steady current of 2 amps to a circuit for 10 seconds. The power delivered is 12 volts times 2 amps, which is 24 watts, and the total energy supplied over that time is 24 watts times 10 seconds, or 240 joules. Now suppose that circuit contains two resistors, and careful analysis shows one dissipates 100 joules over that same interval and the other dissipates 140 joules. Adding those gives 100 plus 140, which equals 240 joules, exactly matching the energy the battery supplied. That match is not a coincidence, it is energy conservation confirming that the circuit analysis was done correctly.

This principle scales up far beyond a single resistor problem. It underlies why engineers can predict battery life from a device's power draw, why a power grid must generate exactly as much electrical energy as everything connected to it consumes at any moment, and why any circuit analysis that leaves energy unaccounted for is a circuit analysis with an error hiding in it somewhere. Whenever you finish solving a circuit, adding up every dissipated power term and comparing it to the total power the sources deliver is a fast, reliable way to catch mistakes before they go any further.
